summary: Two closers running a 30-minute peer roleplay session between live calls. Michael asked to drill the spouse objection ('I need to talk to my wife') chained into the money/uncertainty objection, with Richard playing a 48-year-old married police officer wanting to lose 20-30 lb at $6,000. They ran the sequence twice: the first attempt broke down because Richard kept playing a resistant prospect rather than going along with the script, and Michael stopped to explain he needed to get the words out before he could handle deviation. The second run went through the full responsibility ladder — whose responsibility are the results, the wife's job as an analogy for staying in your own lane, the future-self framing, the nervousness-equals-meaning reframe using the marriage proposal, and the bridge metaphor. Michael ended it saying he had a real call in 12 minutes.
notable: Michael openly stated he does not yet have this script down and was taking a live prospect call twelve minutes later: 'I need to actually be able to say it because I can't. Like, I don't have it down for me.'

The whole drill is aimed at moving a prospect past consulting a spouse about a $6,000 purchase from a shared account. Richard-as-prospect twice grounded the objection in joint finances ('it is money that's in a shared bank account usually') and in money earmarked elsewhere ('I have it, but it's in savings for the kids'), and the scripted response is to reframe consulting the wife as unfair rather than to address the joint-finance reality.

Richard named a live pattern worth a principal's attention: prospects who state joint decision-making as a household rule are, in his experience, near-unwinnable at the close — 'it's so hard with prospects who are like, yeah, that's sort of a rule that we have... I think this is something you have to almost solve in the discovery'.

Michael described the target end-state of the bridge play as a binary between committing and 'settling for mediocrity' — 'Does he step forward and face adversity head-on, or does he crumble and retreat back to mediocrity?'
Richard coached Michael on technique: he pointed out Michael asks hypothetical questions without leaving room for an answer.

Price used throughout the roleplay was $6,000, consistent with the stated offer. Richard-as-prospect referenced '12 hundred people' coached, against the '1,000-plus transformations' figure used on live calls.

Added from the Richard Claessen copy of this meeting (batch_013): the same meeting is recorded twice in Drive, once in each participant's rep folder, under two different file ids. If this duplication pattern extends to sales calls it will double-count them.

Added from the Richard Claessen copy: Michael opened by describing himself as unwell and planning to take calls regardless — 'I'm very tired today. I'm feeling a bit like gray... I can just tell my energy is very, or my mood is very flat. So yeah, show up, take calls, do the thing, sleep.'

Added from the Richard Claessen copy: asked whether his hypothetical questions are meant to be answered, Michael confirmed he cuts the prospect off by design — 'Part of it was I cut it off specifically. I cut it off specifically.'

Added from the Richard Claessen copy: the training method deliberately rehearses the compliant prospect rather than the realistic one. Michael asked Richard to stop resisting — 'I keep feeling like you give me prospects where it's like, they're not going to go along with the roleplay at all. And it's like, bro, I kind of just want to roleplay this out' — and Richard complied for the second run.

Added from the Richard Claessen copy: Michael normalises buyer hesitation as a desirable signal — 'I'd actually be more concerned if you weren't feeling a little bit nervous rather than you feeling a little bit nervous' and 'pretty much every single person I talk to does feel a little bit of nervousness' — and anchors it to the prospect's marriage proposal to argue the nervousness only resolves after committing.
